AI is cracking tough maths problems. How it can bring mathematics closer to cultural studies

It may be too early to say that mathematics will eventually become ‘a branch of Cultural Studies', but following OpenAI’s revelations, researchers in these fields will be spending a lot of time interpreting text.

Subhasish Ray

21 October, 2026 11:14 am IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Representational image | Reuters

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

T his seems as good a moment as any to recall the so-called Sokal Affair. The Spring/Summer 1996 issue of the journal Social Text included an article , titled  Transgressing the Boundaries: Toward a Transformative Hermeneutics of Quantum Gravity . As per Google Scholar, the article currently has over 2000 citations. The author of the article, Alan Sokal, emeritus Physics professor at New York University, subsequently claimed, in a widely read note , that the article was what we would call “slop” in the modern-day.

In an attempt to show a “decline in the standards of intellectual rigor in certain precincts of the American academic humanities”, Sokal wanted to test whether an article “liberally salted with nonsense” — his primary concern was with the use of “scientific and mathematical concepts in ways that few scientists or mathematicians could possibly take seriously” — would pass muster with the editors of a “leading North American journal of cultural studies”  if  “(a) it sounded good and (b) it flattered the editors’ ideological preconceptions.” It did.

“Poor Sokal.” Thus wrote Jacques Derrida, one of the major figures associated with  cultural studies — Derrida pioneered deconstruction, a particular way of approaching texts, which supplied the methodological foundations for the field —  who was subject to a lot of negative press, especially in US newspapers, after the publication of the article. Sokal, Derrida argued, had chosen cheap tricks over a serious engagement with his ideas, noting that he was “always sparing and prudent in the use of scientific references.” Derrida’s admonishments notwithstanding, it was cultural studies that emerged as a lesser force after the Sokal affair, its credibility considerably diminished.

Show Full Article

Thanks to gen erative AI, cultural studies may finally have an answer to the challenge that Sokal had posed three decades ago. At least, that is what Jordana Cepelewicz, Maths editor for the Pulitzer Prize-winning web magazine Quanta seems to suggest, in a recently published article on the platform,  titled Is AI the End of Math As We Know It? .

The crux of the article is that OpenAI’s recent publication of proofs for hundreds of previously unsolved mathematical problems had disrupted the very foundations of mathematics as a discipline because of its obsession with problem-solving and theorem-proving. The article contends that OpenAI’s discoveries meant that the discipline had to reorient itself toward a more interpretative approach, making sense of AI proofs of theorems rather than trying to prove them from scratch.

Also read: India’s IT giants rode labour arbitrage for 30 years. AI is hurting billable hours business model

Navigating ‘language games’ That the field hasn’t taken well to this is perhaps best manifested in the dramatic breakdown of Steven Strogatz, a Maths  professor at Cornell University, over a New York Times podcast. Strogatz went so far as to say that for many in his fraternity, solving theorems gave a “sense of purpose in life” and it grieved him to see that snatched away by gen AI. Cepelewicz, however, goes much further, when she observes that she was “reminded of [the literary theorist] Roland Barthes’ famous 1967 essay ‘The Death of the Author,’ in which he argues that it is the reader, and not the writer, who has ultimate control and agency in actively creating a work’s meaning”.

To see why this is simply an astonishing statement, we need to return to Sokal’s explanation for why he decided to try his “experiment.” Social Text ’s acceptance of his article, he argued, “exemplifies the intellectual arrogance of Theory – meaning postmodernist literary theory – carried to its logical extreme…If all is discourse and ‘text,’ then knowledge of the real world is superfluous; even physics becomes just another branch of Cultural Studies.” Worse still for Sokal, since “all is rhetoric and ‘language games,’ then internal logical consistency is superfluous too: a patina of theoretical sophistication serves equally well.”

While it is too early to say that mathematics, or the mathematically inclined sciences, more generally, will eventually become “a branch of the Cultural Studies,” there should be little doubt that following OpenAI’s extraordinary revelations, researchers in these fields will be spending a lot of time interpreting “text.” Now, of course, there ought to be conventions for doing “good” or “bad” interpretation — Sokal is certainly right that his article should not have been accepted by Social Text — but the “language games” he saw as the exclusive provenance of the humanities is now upon the natural sciences as well.

Moreover, if natural scientists cared to look, there is lots of advice accumulated by the socially oriented sciences on how to navigate these “games.” The important question, as Cepelewicz correctly posits, is whether young mathematicians, raised in higher education systems that have elevated theorem-proving to a higher calling, will be willing to undertake the less celebrated task of interpretation, or vote with their feet.

Subhasish Ray is Professor and Associate Dean of Research at the Jindal School of Government & Public Policy, O.P. Jindal Global University, Haryana. He tweets @subhasish_ray75. Views are personal.

(Edited by Aamaan Alam Khan)

Russia’s failed Great Game is back in Afghanistan

For Russia, the Afghanistan-Pakistan landscape resembles a chessboard. Chess is a two-player game. But those who practise alone know the trick of playing both sides.

Bantirani Patro

21 October, 2026 10:08 am IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Members of Afghanistan's delegation, led by the Taliban-run government's Acting Labour and Social Affairs Minister Abdul Hanan Omari, attend the St. Petersburg International Economic Forum (SPIEF) in Saint Petersburg, Russia June 5, 2024. REUTERS/Anton Vaganov/File Photo

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

L ast week, Russian officials were simultaneously present in Afghanistan, Pakistan and India, suggesting the beginning of another great game along the South Asian frontier, except that Russia no longer has the greatness of its erstwhile empire. Nor does it have a British empire to compete against. But even after decades, the appeal of Afghanistan still remains for Russia.

Russia’s foreign intelligence chief, Sergey Naryshkin , was in Kabul on 14 October to meet the Taliban’s intelligence chief, Abdul Haq Wasiq. The same day, New Delhi hosted the seventh round of the ‘India-Russia Special Mechanism on Pakistan and Afghanistan’. Meanwhile, in Pakistan, Russian interior minister Vladimir Kolokoltsev met the country’s civilian and military leadership, including Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Army Chief Field Marshal Asim Munir. It was the first visit by a Russian interior minister to Pakistan, during which Moscow and Islamabad signed an MoU to strengthen cooperation in combating organised crime.

That three Russian security representatives were in three regional capitals in the same week was unlikely to be a coincidence. Though a full picture of Moscow’s intentions will emerge in the coming months or years, the trajectory is manifest. In this region, Moscow appears to be expanding its role by seeking to mediate between Kabul and Islamabad, all the while coordinating with its time-tested partner New Delhi on the same issue.

Show Full Article

From Soviet invasion to formal recognition The last Soviet soldier left Afghanistan in February 1989. But the invasion’s infamous legacy remains visible in many ways, including the landmines strewn across the country that still kill Afghans. Robert D Kaplan in his Soldiers of God cites a few studies to argue that the Soviet Union killed 1.3 million people in Afghanistan, a toll exceeding the death toll of the Iran-Iraq war and equivalent to the toll of 75 Israeli invasions of Lebanon on the scale of the 1982 invasion.

Today, Russia is back in Afghanistan, not to invade or install a pro-communist government, but to do business with those at the helm. It removed the Taliban from its terrorist list in April 2025, recognised their government that July, and in May 2026, signed a military-technical cooperation agreement with them. Though the terms are not public, reports suggest it covers the repair and maintenance of Russian and Soviet-made equipment. It is a long way from the 1990s, when Moscow backed the Northern Alliance against the first Taliban regime.

The irony is hard to miss. Russia is trying to mediate between the Taliban – heirs of the very mujahideen that drove them out of the country – and Pakistan, which financed, trained, and nurtured them.

For Russia, the Afghanistan-Pakistan landscape resembles a chessboard. Chess is a two-player game. But those who practise alone know the trick of playing both sides. That is Moscow’s current strategy. Any pawn moved from Afghanistan’s side has to be met with another in Pakistan, and Russia must anticipate both carefully. It just so happens that chess is a beloved pastime in Russia.

The point is that both countries have always been interlinked in Russia’s strategic calculations, as they have been in those of many other regional and extra-regional players. For instance, when it was clear that the Soviets were losing to the mujahideen by 1987, their best hope was to “destabilise the guerrillas’ rear base” in Pakistan. Kaplan writes that the US State Department reported over a hundred terrorist incidents in Pakistan cities that year, with Pakistan suffering one third of all the fatalities and one half of the wounded in terrorist attacks worldwide in 1987. A Russia that once exploited the link between the two countries to bleed its enemy now hopes to sustain that link.

Today, Russia seeks a stable Afghanistan where the Islamic State Khorasan Province (ISKP) won’t find breathing space and where instability and chaos do not spill into Central Asian states that Moscow still treats as its sphere of influence. This intent is clear from the head of Russia’s Federal Security Service warning that ISKP, based in Afghanistan, is recruiting members from Central Asian states. A report by Afghanistan International goes even further, claiming that Russia is funding and equipping a special Taliban unit to counter ISKP.

Besides, on October 15-16, Moscow, which holds the chairmanship of the Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO) this year, hosted a joint meeting between the CSTO, the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) and the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS). The theme was security in Central Asia and Afghanistan. Read alongside the three simultaneous visits, Russia’s layered Afghanistan strategy comes through. A larger delegation led by the Russian Deputy Prime Minister is due soon in Afghanistan.

Also read: Moscow Format has become a talk-shop. Afghanistan is receding from global agenda

Russia, an unlikely mediator Afghanistan will not stabilise as long as it remains locked in ‘open war’ with Pakistan. So, Moscow is engaging Islamabad too. But its embrace of the Taliban may complicate matters, as may its reported mediation . If Russia sees the Taliban as a counterterrorism partner in the fight against the ISKP threat, then Pakistan holds the Taliban responsible for terrorism on its soil and for harbouring the Pakistani Taliban. Moscow still acknowledges terrorism emanating from Afghanistan, but it distinguishes that from the Taliban administration.

When fighting erupted along the Afghanistan-Pakistan border earlier this month, the Russian embassy in Kabul tweeted , “We are seriously concerned about the ongoing military confrontation between Pakistan and Afghanistan, which affects civilians, including children”. Many read this as tilting towards the Taliban, which accuses Pakistan of killing civilians in airstrikes in Afghanistan, a charge Pakistan obstinately denies.

Others have tried to play this role. China, Qatar, Turkey and Saudi Arabia have all attempted to mediate between Islamabad and Kabul. At best they have secured temporary ceasefires that were quickly punctured, or agreements without written or verifiable mechanisms. On October 5, the Russia-led Moscow Format Consultations on Afghanistan could not produce a joint communique because of Taliban-Pakistan tensions over terrorism.

Russia, moreover, has historical baggage that it brings to the table as a potential intercessor. Pakistani security analyst Muhammad Amir Rana wrote in a column for Dawn , “Is it not interesting that the conventional wars fought by India and Pakistan collectively may not have lasted for more than a few weeks, and that Pakistan fought its longest war against the Soviet Union in Afghanistan?…The Pakistani leadership still takes pride in that success.”

The present is an obstacle too. If Russia indeed is arming the Taliban, Pakistan may fear the weapons will be turned on it. Russia can still bring both sides to the table. It holds real leverage over the Taliban, which will want to preserve Russian recognition and the cooperation that comes with it, and Pakistan has reason to use Russia’s proximity to the Taliban to give dialogue a chance.

From fighting the mujahideen to courting their successors, Russia is rewriting its place in the region’s history. In some respects, it is whitewashing its past. Whatever the consequence of the current not-so-great game Russia is playing, they will reinforce how short the world’s collective memory of Afghanistan can be.

Bantirani Patro is a staff writer at ThePrint. She tweets @bantirani_patro. Views are personal.

(Edited by Prashant Dixit)

Musk is on a donation spree—SpaceX shares for US kids to $276 million for Republican groups

Musk’s political donations are far higher than those of most individual donors. His plan to give every child in America a SpaceX share could be worth an estimated $10.5 billion.

Sakshi Mehra

20 October, 2026 07:58 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

File photo of multibillionaire tech CEO Elon Musk | Reuters

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: Elon Musk is in a giving mood. Over the past few days, he has announced a plan to give a SpaceX share to every child in America. Meanwhile, newly disclosed filings show he has donated more than $276 million to Republican political groups since July, making him the biggest known donor of the 2026 midterm election cycle.

Musk’s political donations are far higher than those of most individual donors. His plan to give every child in America a SpaceX share could be worth an estimated $10.5 billion.

However, not all the money he has announced has been given. Some are pledges, some are prize money, while others have gone to organisations closely linked to his businesses.

Show Full Article

SpaceX share for every American child

Musk said on 19 October that he would give one of his SpaceX shares to every kid in America next year, calling it “the first of many.”  The plan would cover about 72 million children and is estimated to be worth $10.5 billion, based on SpaceX’s reported share price.

$158 million to Senate Republicans

Musk donated $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund, the main Republican super PAC focused on Senate elections. Much of the money was directed toward supporting Texas Republican Ken Paxton’s Senate campaign.

More than $76 million to America PAC

Musk also gave more than $76 million to America PAC, the political committee he founded in 2024. The PAC is running voter-turnout operations in competitive Senate and House races. As its founder and biggest financial supporter, Musk plays a major role in funding its political activities.

$20 million to House Republicans

Musk donated $20 million to the Congressional Leadership Fund, the leading super PAC supporting Republican candidates for the House of Representatives. The money will support Republican efforts to defend their majority in the House during the midterm elections.

$10 million to Ken Paxton’s Texas campaign

Musk gave $10 million to the Lone Star Liberty PAC, which supports Paxton’s campaign for the US Senate in Texas. Musk lives near SpaceX’s Starbase facility in South Texas, adding a personal and business connection to his political spending in the state.

$10 million to Republican governors

Musk donated $10 million to the Republican Governors Association, which supports Republican candidates running for governor across the US.

$2 million to Republican attorneys general

Musk gave $2 million to the Republican Attorneys General Association, which supports Republican candidates for state attorney general offices. These officials can play an important role in legal challenges to federal policies, making the association another part of Musk’s political giving.

$500,000 to Greg Abbott

Earlier in 2026, Musk donated $500,000 to Texans for Governor Greg Abbott, according to Texas campaign-finance filings. The contribution was made during the first six months of the year and adds to his financial support for Republican politicians in Texas.

(Edited by Aamaan Alam Khan)
